title: "Software Fundamentals Matter More Than Ever" — Matt Pocock

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is coding agents and software-engineering practices for using AI to generate, test, and architect code. The content centers on software-engineering assistants for coding with AI while the principles discussed are broadly applicable. The talk covers planning via Grill Me and ubiquitous language, implementation via TDD, and maintenance via deep module refactoring. The talk assumes familiarity with software engineering fundamentals and references multiple foundational texts. This is a conference talk delivered at the AI Engineer event. All evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Matt Pocock opens by reassuring developers that their skills remain valuable, arguing software fundamentals matter more than ever. He critiques the specs-to-code movement—writing specs, letting AI generate code, and only modifying specs when problems arise. His experience showed this produces progressively worse code each iteration, calling it vibe coding by another name. He references John Osterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design for its definition of complexity, The Pragmatic Programmer on software entropy, and Frederick P. Brooks' The Design of Design on design concepts. The core thesis: good codebases matter more because AI performs well in them but poorly in bad ones, making bad code the most expensive it's ever been. He then addresses failure modes with AI coding. First, when AI doesn't do what you wanted—he introduces his Grill Me skill, which interviews the developer relentlessly (40 to 100+ questions) until reaching shared understanding. Second, when AI is too verbose—he connects this to Domain-Driven Design's ubiquitous language concept; his skill scans the codebase for terminology and creates a markdown reference file. Third, when AI builds the right thing but it doesn't work—he recommends feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests. He notes LLMs do too much at once, outrunning their headlights, and TDD forces small deliberate steps. He then connects testability to Osterhout's deep modules concept: few large modules with simple interfaces that hide complexity, versus shallow modules that are hard for AI to explore. His improve-codebase-architecture skill helps restructure code into deep modules. He introduces a fifth tip: design the interface, delegate the implementation—treating deep modules as gray boxes where you control the interface but let AI handle internals. This reduces cognitive load compared to shallow-module codebases where both developer and AI must hold everything in their heads. He emphasizes modules must be part of your ubiquitous language and built into planning skills, citing Kent Beck's advice to invest in the design of the system every day. The closing message: code is not cheap, AI is a tactical programmer (a sergeant on the ground), and developers must operate at the strategic level using decades-old software fundamentals.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening and Thesis: Software Fundamentals Matter More Than Ever
sections.summary: Pocock opens by reassuring developers that their skills remain valuable, stating that software fundamentals matter now more than ever. He introduces his course Clojure Code for Real Engineers and notes the challenge of building an AI coding curriculum in a rapidly changing landscape.

sections.title: Critique of Specs-to-Code and Why Code Is Not Cheap
sections.summary: Pocock critiques the specs-to-code movement, sharing his experience of getting progressively worse code with each iteration. He references Osterhout's complexity definition and The Pragmatic Programmer's software entropy concept. He argues bad code is the most expensive it's ever been because it blocks AI's benefits, establishing the talk's thesis: good codebases matter more than ever.

sections.title: Failure Mode 1: AI Didn't Do What I Wanted — Grill Me Skill
sections.summary: Pocock addresses the failure mode where AI produces something unwanted, attributing it to not sharing a design concept (from Brooks). He introduces the Grill Me skill, which interviews the developer relentlessly (40-100+ questions) until shared understanding is reached. The repo has ~13,000 stars. He considers this better than default plan mode in Clojure Code.

sections.title: Failure Mode 2: AI Too Verbose — Ubiquitous Language Skill
sections.summary: Pocock connects AI verbosity to the language gap between developers and domain experts, citing DDD's ubiquitous language concept. His skill scans the codebase for terminology and creates a markdown reference file. This improves planning, reduces AI verbosity, and aligns implementation with plans.

sections.title: Failure Mode 3: AI Built Right Thing But It Doesn't Work — TDD and Feedback Loops
sections.summary: Pocock recommends feedback loops: static types (TypeScript), browser access for frontend apps, and automated tests. He notes LLMs don't use feedback loops well, doing too much at once (outrunning your headlights). TDD forces small steps: create test, make it pass, refactor. He notes testing is hard due to interdependent decisions about unit size, mocking, and behaviors to test.

sections.title: Deep Modules and Testable Codebases
sections.summary: Pocock connects testability to Osterhout's deep modules concept: few large modules with simple interfaces that hide complexity, versus shallow modules with complex interfaces and little functionality. Shallow-module codebases are hard for AI to explore and understand. His improve-codebase-architecture skill helps restructure code into deep modules, creating testable boundaries at interfaces.

sections.title: Design the Interface, Delegate the Implementation
sections.summary: Pocock introduces his fifth tip: design the interface and delegate the implementation. Deep modules can be treated as gray boxes—control the interface, let AI handle internals, test from outside. This reduces cognitive load versus shallow-module codebases. Modules must be part of ubiquitous language and built into planning skills. He cites Kent Beck's advice to invest in system design every day, contrasting with specs-to-code which divests from design.

sections.title: Closing: Code Is Not Cheap and Developers Must Think Strategically
sections.summary: Pocock closes by emphasizing code is not cheap and code is important. He frames AI as a tactical programmer (a sergeant on the ground) while developers must operate at the strategic level using decades-old software fundamentals. He points to his GitHub repo mattpocockskills for the skills mentioned and promotes his training and newsletter at aihero.dev.
